intro: Balfron's Clachan Oak is known locally as the hanging tree. Iron hoops hold its hollow trunk together, and a local visitor guide says people were once chained to it as punishment for petty crimes. The same guide dates it to at least 1553, and local legend ties it to William Wallace and Rob Roy MacGregor, though one account doubts it is old enough for Wallace. It stands in the old part of the village, the Clachan, about 28 kilometres from Stirling, with no gate or fee reported.
meta_description: The Clachan Oak in Balfron, the hoop-bound hanging tree said to date to at least 1553: its story, its legends and where to find it.
question_meta: Balfron's oldest tree is the Clachan Oak, the hoop-bound hanging tree thought to date back to at least 1553.
question_answer: The Clachan Oak is Balfron's oldest tree, thought by a local visitor guide to date back to at least 1553, which would make it more than 470 years old. Nobody has published a girth or a scientific age to confirm it.

Iron hoops hold its hollow trunk together, and a local visitor guide says people were once chained to it as punishment for petty crimes. The same guide says it is thought to date back to at least 1553 and possibly further, without saying where the date comes from, so it is the local account rather than a measurement. Legend asks more of it. Local stories tie the oak to William Wallace and to Rob Roy MacGregor, but one account thinks it unlikely the tree is old enough for Wallace, who died in 1305. It was photographed in November 2012, the hoops plain on its trunk, and again in February 2022, and an observation logged at the spot in 2025 suggests it still stands. trees.story:
Balfron calls this the hanging tree. Iron hoops hold its hollow trunk together, and according to a local visitor guide, people were once chained to it as punishment for petty crimes.

It stands in the Clachan, in the village of Balfron, and the same guide says it is thought to date back to at least 1553, possibly further. That would put it past 470 years. The guide does not say where the date comes from, so read it as the local account rather than a measurement. Nobody has published a girth or a height.

Legend asks more of it. Local stories tie the oak to William Wallace and to Rob Roy MacGregor. One account thinks it unlikely the tree is old enough for Wallace, who died in 1305, and that is the reading we would trust.

What is not in doubt is that it is still here. It was photographed in November 2012, its hoops plain on the trunk, and again in February 2022, and an observation logged at the spot in 2025 suggests it stands today.

We have not confirmed the species beyond oak. If you can tell whether it is pedunculate or sessile, tell us which, and if you know where the 1553 date comes from, we would like to hear that too.

It stands in the village with no gate or fee reported. Balfron is about 28 kilometres from Stirling, so this is a trip of its own rather than a detour from the city.
trees.access: Standing in the village (The Clachan); no gate or entry fee reported in sources, not confirmed on the ground
trees.transport: Balfron village bus from Stirling, roughly 40 to 50 minutes (not verified); outside the 30 minute day-trip band
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the iron hoops that hold its hollow trunk together. It stands in the Clachan, the old part of Balfron village.
